## 3.1 The wavefront carries wavelength, frequency, phase, and action

The McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic predicts that the advance of x₄ is a wavefront, and a wavefront has a wavelength, a frequency, a phase, and an action per cycle; the three theorems of this subsection make that prediction exact.

**Theorem 3.1 (Periodicity and action are properties of the wavefront).** *Let x₄ advance as a spherically symmetric wavefront at speed c. Then (i) the wavefront has a wavelength λ and a frequency f with λ f = c; (ii) the phase φ of a matter wavefront is an action divided by a quantum of action, φ = S/ħ, so the wavefront carries an action per cycle, h = 2πħ; (iii) the action per cycle is one constant for every x₄-wavefront, Planck's constant h, because the Principle states one spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere at every event whose wavelength sets the action h: the universality of h is in the Principle, as the universality of c is.*

*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of x₄ at c, dx₄/dt = ic. (i) A wavefront is a surface of constant phase of a periodic disturbance; a periodic disturbance propagating at c has λ f = c. (ii) For a matter wave the phase is S/ħ (de Broglie 1924 [34]; Hamilton–Jacobi), equivalently E = hf, p = h/λ; a wavefront carrying phase therefore has a nonzero action per cycle, and naming it h identifies the action quantum with a property of the wavefront's own periodicity. (iii) The Principle, as stated at the head of this section, is one statement: a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere at every event, expanding at c, whose wavelength sets the action h. The same clause that makes c the rate at every event makes h the action per cycle at every event; there is one x₄-wavefront structure, so there is one wavelength and one action per cycle, and that constant is Planck's. ∎ **G1** for (i)–(iii). The action is in the Principle; c and h are the two dimensional constants of the one advance, its rate and its action per cycle, joined by λ f = c.

**Theorem 3.2 (Phase and oscillation are geometry of the i).** *Write the increment of the Principle as dx₄ = ic dt. Then (i) ic = c e^{iπ/2}: each increment is a quarter-turn; (ii) on the base coordinate the increment sums to the straight advance x₄ = ict, d²x₄/dt² = 0, while on a phase ψ riding the advance it acts multiplicatively, ψ ↦(1 + i ω dt)ψ, each increment turning the phase by a quarter-turn; (iii) compounding gives lim_{n→∞}(1 + iθ/n)ⁿ = e^{iθ}, periodic with d² e^{iω t}/dt² = -ω² e^{iω t} and closure i⁴ = 1; (iv) a real advance dx₄/dt = c gives e^{ct}, d² e^{ct}/dt² = +c² e^{ct}, with no oscillation. The wave character of matter comes from the quarter-turn i — the perpendicularity of the fourth axis — and the scale of the oscillation is the action per cycle h that the Principle's wavelength sets (Theorem 3.1).*

*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of x₄ at c, dx₄/dt = ic. (i) i = cos(π/2) + isin(π/2) = e^{iπ/2}, so ic = c e^{iπ/2}. (ii) x₄(t) = ∫₀^t ic ds = ict, whose second derivative vanishes; on the fibre, ψ(t + dt) = ψ(t) + iω dt ψ(t), and at ψ = 1 the increment iω dt is purely imaginary, i.e. at right angles to 1 in the complex plane. (iii) (1 + iθ/n)ⁿ = exp(nlog(1 + iθ/n)) = exp(iθ + O(1/n)) →e^{iθ}; (d²)/(dt²)e^{iω t} = (iω)² e^{iω t} = -ω² e^{iω t}; i⁴ = (i²)² = (-1)² = 1. (iv) (d²)/(dt²)e^{ct} = c² e^{ct} > 0, monotone. ∎ **G1.**

**Theorem 3.3 (The Compton clock).** *A particle of rest mass m at spatial rest places its whole budget into the x₄-advance (Theorem 2.3). Its rest energy E = mc² is, by E = ħω (Theorem 3.1), a frequency*

ω_C = (mc²)/ħ, λ_C = h/(mc), (3.1)

*the Compton frequency and Compton wavelength — the rate at which the wavefront of dx₄/dt = ic advances the phase of a rest-mass-m standing wave. The rest-frame phase is e^{-iω_C t}; written on the coordinate x₄ = ict it is the real exponential e^{-mc x₄/ħ}, the Wick relationship between oscillation in t and exponential behaviour along x₄ [11].*

*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of x₄ at c, dx₄/dt = ic. E = mc² at rest; E = ħω from Theorem 3.1(ii); λ_C = c/f_C = 2π c/ω_C = h/mc. For the Wick form substitute t = x₄/(ic): e^{-iω_C t} = e^{-iω_C x₄/(ic)} = e^{-ω_C x₄/c} = e^{-mc x₄/ħ}. ∎ **G1.**

**Corollary 3.3a (The action per Compton cycle is h).** *For a particle of rest mass m at spatial rest, the action accumulated by the wavefront phase over one Compton period T_C = 2π/ω_C is S_C = E T_C = mc²·2πħ/(mc²) = 2πħ= h, independent of m. The McGucken Sphere's wavelength therefore sets the action h: one cycle of the wavefront's phase carries exactly one quantum of action, for every mass.*

*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of x₄ at c, dx₄/dt = ic. The rest-frame phase is φ = S/ħ= -ω_C t (Theorem 3.3), so over T_C the phase advances by 2π and S by 2πħ= h; with E = ħω_C this is E T_C. ∎ **G1** given Theorem 3.1(ii); the statement that the same h serves every wavefront is Theorem 3.1(iii). This is the sense of the Principle anchor's clause "whose wavelength sets the action h": the Compton wavelength λ_C = h/mc and the Compton period T_C = h/mc² are the one quantum h divided by the particle's momentum scale mc and energy scale mc² respectively.

## 3.2 The Klein–Gordon equation through both channels

The McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic predicts that the relativistic wave equation for a spin-0 field is the self-consistency condition on the superposition of McGucken Spheres (the Geometric Channel) and, equivalently, the mass-shell Casimir of the metric's translation generators (the Algebraic Channel); both derivations follow.

**Theorem 3.4 (Klein–Gordon from the wavefront — the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel).** *Let matter of rest mass m be a phase structure carried on the spherically symmetric x₄-wavefront, with the interval (2.1). Then the field ψ satisfies*

(1/(c²)(∂²)/(∂t²) - ∇² + (m²c²)/(ħ²))ψ = 0. (3.2)


*Proof, in six steps, each a property of the advance.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of x₄ at c, dx₄/dt = ic.

*Step 1 (mass shell from the budget).* Theorem 2.3 gives the saturated budget u^μ u_μ = -c² in the signature of (2.1). Multiplying by m², the four-momentum p^μ = m u^μ obeys p^μ p_μ = -m²c², i.e. E² = p²c² + m²c⁴.

*Step 2 (Compton frequency).* By Theorem 3.3 the rest-frame oscillation is ω_C = mc²/ħ. Writing k^μ = p^μ/ħ, the mass shell reads k^μ k_μ = -m²c²/ħ² in every frame, by the Lorentz covariance of (2.1).

*Step 3 (plane-wave mode).* The phase accumulated along a straight worldline is S = ∫p_μ dx^μ, so an elementary mode of the Sphere expansion is ψ(x) = exp(i k_ν x^ν) = exp(iS/ħ): the phase is the action carried by the advance, measured in the ħ the advance itself sets (Theorem 3.1).

*Step 4 (the generator squared).* The first-order x₄-generator acts on the rest-frame mode as dψ/dt = -iω_Cψ; its square gives d²ψ/dt² = -ω_C²ψ, the rest-frame form of (3.2). The covariant operator whose rest-frame reduction is d²/dt² is the d'Alembertian of the metric (2.1). On the mode of Step 3, ((1/c²)∂ₜ² - ∇²)exp(i(k·x - ω t)) = (-ω²/c² + |k|²)ψ (Appendix A, check 17), which with Step 2 is -(m²c²/ħ²)ψ; hence (3.2). The mass term is the squared Compton frequency of the x₄-advance, obtained by squaring the first-order generator.

*Step 5 (Huygens–Fresnel–Kirchhoff form).* Write L ≡1/(c²)∂ₜ² - ∇² + κ², κ = mc/ħ, and let G_{ret}(x, x') be the retarded fundamental solution, Lₓ G_{ret}(x,x') = δ⁴(x - x'), G_{ret} = 0 for t < t'. For ψ with Lψ = 0 and any spacetime region Ω bounded by a Cauchy surface Σ in its past, Green's second identity ∫_Ω(ψ Lₓ G - G Lψ) d⁴x = ∮_{∂Ω}(ψ ∂ₙ G - G ∂ₙψ) dΣ (with the t-derivative weighted by 1/c²) gives, for an event x in Ω,

ψ(x) = ∫_Σ [ G_{ret}(x,x') ∂_{n'}ψ(x') - ψ(x') ∂_{n'}G_{ret}(x,x') ] dΣ', (3.2a)

the Kirchhoff–Helmholtz representation: the field at x is the superposition, over the points x' of the Cauchy surface, of the secondary waves G_{ret}(x,x') emitted from each x'. The retarded solution is supported in the forward null cone of x': for m = 0 exactly on the cone, G_{ret} = δ(c(t - t') - |x - x'|)/(4π|x - x'|) — Huygens' principle in its sharp form, the secondary wave being the McGucken Sphere M⁺_{x'}(t) itself; for m > 0 the support includes the cone's interior with the Bessel-function tail -(κ)/(4π) J₁(κ s)/s on s = √{c²(t-t')² - |x-x'|²}, which is the standing x₄-oscillation of Theorem 3.3 trailing the Sphere (Hadamard's characterization of the sharp case, cited in Section 12). Conversely, if ψ is defined by (3.2a) from Cauchy data on Σ, then Lψ = ∫_Σ [δ⁴∂_{n'}ψ - ψ ∂_{n'}δ⁴] dΣ' = 0 off Σ: the superposition of secondary Spheres is self-consistent exactly when each mode satisfies Step 4. The Geometric Channel therefore has a differential face (Step 4) and an integral face (3.2a). McGucken differs from the Huygens–Kirchhoff–Hadamard prior art in providing a physical mechanism for Huygens' principle: x₄'s spherical expansion at c from every event is the secondary wave G_{ret}(x,x') (Section 12).

*Step 6 (massless limit).* At m = 0 the mass shell collapses onto the null cone, k^μ k_μ = 0, and (3.2) becomes the wave equation: the mode propagates on the null cone at c with no Compton frequency — the photon, at absolute rest in x₄ (Theorem 2.3). ∎ **G1** for Steps 1–4 and 6 (the covariant lift in Step 4 is standard Lorentz covariance applied to the metric the Principle produces); **G2** for the universality of ħ (Theorem 3.1(iii)); Step 5 is the integral restatement of Step 4.

**Theorem 3.5 (Klein–Gordon by symmetry — the dx₄/dt = ic Algebraic Channel).** *Translation invariance of the metric (2.1) makes the four-momentum p_μ the conserved generator of spacetime translations (Noether). On the mode ψ = exp(iS/ħ) of Theorem 3.4 that generator is represented by p_μ ↦-iħ∂_μ, since -iħ∂_μ exp(iS/ħ) = (∂_μ S)exp(iS/ħ) = p_μ exp(iS/ħ). Substituting into the mass-shell Casimir p^μ p_μ = -m²c² gives -ħ²∂^μ∂_μψ = -m²c²ψ, which is (3.2).*

*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of x₄ at c, dx₄/dt = ic. For the mode ψ = exp(ik_ν x^ν) with k_ν = p_ν/ħ, ∂_μψ = ik_μψ, so -iħ∂_μψ = ħk_μψ = p_μψ: on every mode the translation generator p_μ acts as -iħ∂_μ, and by linearity on every superposition of modes. Then p^μ p_μψ = (-iħ)² g^{μν}∂_μ∂_νψ = -ħ²(1/(c²)∂ₜ² - ∇²)ψ with the index raised by g = diag(+1,-1,-1,-1), x⁰ = ct (Convention 4.3), for which p^μ p_μ = E²/c² - |p|² and the mass shell of Theorem 3.4, Step 1, reads p^μ p_μ = m²c² (the sign-reversed form in the signature of (2.1), -ħ²η^{μν}∂_μ∂_νψ = -m²c²ψ, is the same equation); this gives -ħ²(1/(c²)∂ₜ² - ∇²)ψ = m²c²ψ, which is (3.2). The canonical-quantization rule p_μ ↦-iħ∂_μ of the textbooks is thus read off the wavefront phase [12]. ∎ **G1.** The two channels reach (3.2) by independent routes — the Algebraic Channel as the image of the Poincaré Casimir on the generators, the Geometric Channel as the self-consistency of the Sphere superposition — and agree.

**Theorem 3.6 (The Schrödinger equation as the slow envelope).** *Write ψ(x,t) = φ(x,t) e^{-imc²t/ħ}, separating the Compton phase from an envelope φ. Substitution into (3.2) gives, exactly,*

1/(c²)(∂²φ)/(∂t²) - (2im)/ħ(∂φ)/(∂t) - ∇²φ = 0, (3.3)

*the two mass terms cancelling identically (Appendix A, check 18). When the envelope varies slowly on the Compton time scale, |∂ₜ²φ| ≪(mc²/ħ)|∂ₜφ|, the first term drops and*

iħ(∂φ)/(∂t) = -(ħ²)/(2m)∇²φ, (3.4)

*the free Schrödinger equation; a scalar potential V enters through minimal coupling, iħ∂ₜφ = [-(ħ²/2m)∇² + V]φ.*

*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of x₄ at c, dx₄/dt = ic. With ψ = φ e^{-iω_C t}, ω_C = mc²/ħ: ∂ₜψ = (∂ₜφ - iω_Cφ)e^{-iω_C t} and ∂ₜ²ψ = (∂ₜ²φ - 2iω_C∂ₜφ - ω_C²φ)e^{-iω_C t}. Substituting into (3.2) and dividing by e^{-iω_C t}: 1/(c²)∂ₜ²φ - (2iω_C)/(c²)∂ₜφ - (ω_C²)/(c²)φ - ∇²φ + (m²c²)/(ħ²)φ = 0. Since ω_C²/c² = m²c²/ħ² the two mass terms cancel, and 2ω_C/c² = 2m/ħ gives (3.3). Dropping 1/(c²)∂ₜ²φ under the stated condition leaves -(2im)/ħ∂ₜφ = ∇²φ, i.e. ∂ₜφ = (iħ)/(2m)∇²φ; multiplying by iħ gives iħ∂ₜφ = -(ħ²)/(2m)∇²φ, which is (3.4). ∎ **G1.** In the Geometric Channel, (3.4) is the slow envelope diffusing by Huygens superposition over the spatial Spheres, the imaginary diffusion coefficient iħ/2m being the residue of the wavefront's phase advance; in the Algebraic Channel, it is the nonrelativistic contraction of the Poincaré Casimir to the Galilean one [1]. Nonrelativistic quantum mechanics is downstream of the same advance: c, ħ, and the phase were fixed by dx₄/dt = ic before any wave equation was written.

# 4. The Clifford Algebra of the McGucken Interval

The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension x₄ is expanding at the velocity of light: dx₄/dt = ic, with x₄ = ict, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action h and whose volume defines a nonlocality.

*In the author's words — reproduced verbatim and in full from [5], §II.3, §II.4 (the Dirac paper; verified-read). Equation and reference numbers are those of [5].*

**II.3 The 4D Clifford Algebra**

Given the Minkowski signature derived in II.1, any first-order wave operator that squares to the Klein–Gordon operator (derived from the wavefront in II.5–II.6) must satisfy the Clifford algebra:


{γ^u, γ^v} = 2η^{uv} 𝟙


where {·,·} denotes the anticommutator, η = diag(−1, +1, +1, +1), and 𝟙 is the identity on the representation space. In the remainder of the paper we follow the common convention of suppressing the identity matrix where context makes it clear. This is the Clifford algebra Cl(1,3). Its minimal faithful representation is 4-dimensional, and the objects it acts on are Dirac spinors. A detailed derivation of this result from the Light, Time, Dimension Theory principle is given in the companion paper on Clifford algebra from dx₄/dt = ic.

We take the γ-matrices as given for what follows and focus on the geometric origin of their spinorial action.

**II.4 Convention Statement**

The results of this paper, in particular the component-level calculation in Section VIII, depend on explicit choices of basis conventions. We fix them here and use them consistently throughout.

**Pauli matrix convention:** σ₁, σ₂, σ₃ are the standard Hermitian Pauli matrices with σᵢσⱼ = δᵢⱼ 𝟙 + iεᵢⱼₖ σₖ, where εᵢⱼₖ is the totally antisymmetric symbol with ε₁₂₃ = +1 (physics convention).

**Bivector-to-Pauli identification:** Under the isomorphism between the even subalgebra of Cl(0,3) and 2×2 complex matrices, we identify:

e₂₃ ↔ −iσ₁, e₃₁ ↔ −iσ₂, e₁₂ ↔ −iσ₃

This sign choice ensures that exp(θ/2 · e₁₂) acting on a spin-up state along the z-axis produces the standard rotation by angle θ about that axis.

**Gamma matrix basis:** Except where explicitly stated, we work in the Weyl (chiral) basis, in which the γ-matrices take the form:


γ⁰ = [[0, 𝟙₂], [𝟙₂, 0]], γⁱ = [[0, σⁱ], [-σⁱ, 0]], γ⁵ = [[-𝟙₂, 0], [0, 𝟙₂]]


where each block is 2×2 and 𝟙₂ is the 2×2 identity.

**Pseudoscalar:** I ≡ γ⁰γ¹γ²γ³ (sometimes denoted γ⁵ up to sign conventions; we write I when we mean the Clifford pseudoscalar and γ⁵ when we mean the chirality operator, with their relationship given explicitly where needed).

**Charge conjugation matrix:** In the Weyl basis, the standard choice is C = iγ²γ⁰, satisfying C⁻¹γᵘC = −(γᵘ)ᵀ and Cᵀ = −C. We use this convention in Section VIII.

These choices fix all signs and normalizations in the component calculation.

*(End of the passage from [5], §II.3, §II.4.)*

*In the author's words — reproduced verbatim and in full from [6], §3.1 (the spinor paper; verified-read). Equation and reference numbers are those of [6].*

**3.1 First root (Clifford/Dirac): the vector square-roots the scalar interval**

**Theorem 3.1 (Clifford root).** *Let {γ^μ} satisfy the Clifford relation {γ^μ, γ^ν} = 2η^μν 𝟙. Then for any four-momentum p_μ,*

> (γ^μ p_μ)² = (p²) 𝟙 = (η^μν p_μ p_ν) 𝟙,   …(3.1)

*and the Dirac operator D = iγ^μ∂_μ satisfies D² = −□. The first-order operator D is a square root of the second-order Klein–Gordon operator.*

*Proof.* (γ^μ p_μ)(γ^ν p_ν) = ½{γ^μ, γ^ν}p_μp_ν = η^μν p_μp_ν 𝟙, since p_μp_ν is symmetric so only the symmetric part ½{γ^μ,γ^ν} contributes. Setting p_μ ↦ −i∂_μ gives D² = −η^μν∂_μ∂_ν = −□. ∎

Verified symbolically in the Weyl basis: {γ_μ,γ_ν} − 2η_μν𝟙 = 0 for all sixteen index pairs, and (γ^μ p_μ)² − (p₀²−p₁²−p₂²−p₃²)𝟙 = 0 identically. The vector γ^μ is, in the sense of (3.1), the square root of the scalar metric. **G1.**

*(End of the passage from [6], §3.1.)*

**Theorem 4.1 (The Clifford relation is forced on any first-order square root of Klein–Gordon).** *Let D = Γ^μ∂_μ be a first-order operator with constant coefficient matrices Γ^μ, and demand D² = g^{μν}∂_μ∂_ν 𝟙 for a symmetric g^{μν}. Then*

{Γ^μ, Γ^ν} = 2 g^{μν} 𝟙. (4.1)

*For the Klein–Gordon operator of (3.2), g = diag(+1,-1,-1,-1) in units with x⁰ = ct.*

*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of x₄ at c, dx₄/dt = ic. D² = Γ^μΓ^ν∂_μ∂_ν = ½{Γ^μ,Γ^ν}∂_μ∂_ν, since ∂_μ∂_ν is symmetric and only the symmetric part of Γ^μΓ^ν survives. Equating to g^{μν}∂_μ∂_ν𝟙 for all second derivatives gives (4.1). ∎ **G1.**

**Theorem 4.2 (Dimension of the spinor space).** *The complex algebra generated by four elements satisfying (4.1) for a nondegenerate g is the full matrix algebra M₄(ℂ) of dimension 16. Its unique irreducible module has complex dimension 4. The Dirac spinor is therefore a four-component complex object, and the sixteen products 𝟙, γ^μ, γ^μγ^ν (μ<ν), γ^μγ^νγ^ρ (μ<ν<ρ), γ⁰γ¹γ²γ³ form a basis of M₄(ℂ).*

*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of x₄ at c, dx₄/dt = ic. (a) *The sixteen ordered products span the algebra.* Any word in the generators reduces, by repeated use of (4.1) — Γ^μΓ^ν = -Γ^νΓ^μ for μ ≠ν and (Γ^μ)² = g^{μμ}𝟙 — to a scalar multiple of an ordered product Γ^{μ₁}⋯Γ^{μₖ} with μ₁ < …< μₖ, 0 ≤ k ≤ 4. There are 2⁴ = 16 such products, so the complex algebra 𝒜 generated by the Γ^μ has dimension at most 16. (b) *They are linearly independent in the Weyl realization.* Let Γ_A, A = 1,…,16, be the ordered products of the matrices (4.2). Each Γ_A with A ≠𝟙 is traceless: for a product of k ≥ 1 distinct generators, choose a generator γ^ν not in the product if k < 4 (then γ^νΓ_A(γ^ν)⁻¹ = (-1)^kΓ_A, and for k odd the trace vanishes by cyclicity; for k even choose instead a generator γ^ρ in the product, write Γ_A = ±γ^ρΓ' with Γ' a product of k-1 generators anticommuting with γ^ρ, and tr(γ^ρΓ') = tr(Γ'γ^ρ) = -tr(γ^ρΓ')), and for k = 4, tr(γ⁰γ¹γ²γ³) = 0 by the same anticommutation. Moreover Γ_AΓ_B = c_{AB}Γ_C with c_{AB} ∈{±1, ±i} and Γ_C = 𝟙 only when A = B, since Γ_A² = ±𝟙. Hence tr(Γ_AΓ_B) = 0 for A ≠B and tr(Γ_A²) = ±4: the Γ_A are orthogonal under the trace form and therefore linearly independent. (c) *Conclusion.* By (a) and (b), dim𝒜 = 16 = dim M₄(ℂ), and the Weyl realization is a surjective homomorphism 𝒜 →M₄(ℂ), hence an isomorphism. M₄(ℂ) acts irreducibly on ℂ⁴ (it contains every matrix unit), and every finite-dimensional module of Mₙ(ℂ) is a direct sum of copies of ℂⁿ (Wedderburn's theorem for a simple algebra; this one standard fact is cited), so the irreducible module is unique. (d) *Convention independence.* If {Γ^μ,Γ^ν} = 2g^{μν} then Γ'^μ = iΓ^μ satisfies {Γ'^μ,Γ'^ν} = -2g^{μν}, so over ℂ the two sign conventions generate the same algebra. (Appendix A, check 1, verifies (4.1) for (4.2).) ∎ **G1** (one cited standard fact, Wedderburn, named as such).

**Convention 4.3 (Matrix convention, fixed and named).** Throughout, the matrix generators are the Weyl (chiral) matrices

γ⁰ = [0, 𝟙₂; 𝟙₂, 0], γⁱ = [0, σⁱ; -σⁱ, 0], γ⁵ = iγ⁰γ¹γ²γ³ = [-𝟙₂, 0; 0, 𝟙₂], (4.2)

with σⁱ the Pauli matrices, σⁱσ^j = δ^{ij}𝟙 + iε^{ijk}σ^k. These satisfy {γ^μ,γ^ν} = 2g^{μν}𝟙 with g = diag(+1,-1,-1,-1), so (γ⁰)² = +𝟙 and (γⁱ)² = -𝟙. The interval of Theorem 2.1 is ds² = -g_{μν}dx^μ dx^ν; the generators of the Clifford algebra of the (-,+,+,+) form are e_μ = -iγ_μ, with eᵢ² = +1, e₄² = -1. The overall sign of the quadratic form is a convention; both signs give the same complex algebra M₄(ℂ) (Theorem 4.2), the same bivector squares (Theorem 4.4), the same pseudoscalar up to sign, and the same component calculation (Theorem 10.2). The source paper [5] states the (-,+,+,+) relation in its §II.3 while using the matrices (4.2) in its §II.4 and §VIII; the present paper fixes the convention to the matrices and so to g.

**Theorem 4.4 (Bivector squares: compact rotations and non-compact boosts).** *For the spatial bivectors (γⁱγ^j)² = -𝟙 (i ≠j); for the bivectors containing the x₄ direction, (γ⁰γⁱ)² = +𝟙. The spatial bivectors generate compact (periodic) rotations and the x₄-involving bivectors generate non-compact boosts of unbounded rapidity. The split traces to the i of dx₄/dt = ic through the signature of Theorem 2.1.*

*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of x₄ at c, dx₄/dt = ic. (γ¹γ²)² = γ¹γ²γ¹γ² = -(γ¹)²(γ²)² = -(-1)(-1) = -𝟙; (γ⁰γ¹)² = -(γ⁰)²(γ¹)² = -(+1)(-1) = +𝟙 (Appendix A, check 3). In the e_μ convention the same squares follow from eᵢ² = +1, e₄² = -1. ∎ **G1.**

**Theorem 4.5 (The pseudoscalar).** *Let I ≡γ⁰γ¹γ²γ³. Then I² = -𝟙; I anticommutes with every vector γ^μ; I commutes with every bivector γ^μγ^ν and hence with every element of the even subalgebra Cl⁺. In the Weyl basis I = -iγ⁵.*

*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of x₄ at c, dx₄/dt = ic. I² = -𝟙 by direct multiplication. Moving γ^μ through the four factors of I it anticommutes with three and commutes with itself: γ^μ I = (-1)³ Iγ^μ. A bivector is a product of two vectors, so it picks up (-1)² = +1; the even subalgebra is spanned by 𝟙, the six bivectors, and I. Appendix A, check 2, verifies all of this for (4.2). ∎ **G1.** The pseudoscalar is the geometric embodiment, in Cl(1,3), of the i of dx₄/dt = ic: it is the unit 4-volume element, squares to -1, and is central on the even subalgebra where the matter field lives (Section 7). That the i of the quantum phase is this I, which is the i of the Principle, is the identification the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework carries (**G2**); the algebra of I is **G1**.

# 5. The Square-Root Tower: The Spinor as the Fourth Root of the McGucken Interval

The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension x₄ is expanding at the velocity of light: dx₄/dt = ic, with x₄ = ict, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action h and whose volume defines a nonlocality.

*In the author's words — reproduced verbatim and in full from [6], §3.2, §3.3, §4., §5., §5.3 (the spinor paper; verified-read). Equation and reference numbers are those of [6].*

**3.2 Second root (Fierz/twistor): the spinor square-roots the vector**

**Theorem 3.2 (Fierz root).** *The Dirac current j^μ = ψ̄γ^μψ is a four-vector that is quadratic (bilinear) in ψ. For a single Weyl spinor λ_a, the hermitian matrix p_{aȧ} = λ_a λ̄_ȧ is the σ-image of a four-vector p^μ, and p^μ is null.*

*Proof.* j^μ carries one vector index built from two spinor indices contracted through γ^μ — the k = 1 entry of the Fierz/Cartan classification (§4). For the Weyl case, p_{aȧ} = λ_a λ̄_ȧ has det(λλ†) = 0 identically (rank one). Under the soldering p_{aȧ} = p_μ(σ^μ)_{aȧ}, p² = det(p_{aȧ}) up to fixed normalization, hence p² = 0. ∎

Verified symbolically: with λ = (a, b)ᵀ, det(λλ†) = 0 identically, and p^μ = ½ tr(σ^μ λλ†) gives p_t² − p_x² − p_y² − p_z² = 0 identically. The spinor is the square root of a null vector. **G1.**

**3.3 Composition: the interval is quartic in the spinor**

**Theorem 3.3 (Quartic interval / fourth root).** *Composing 3.1 and 3.2, the interval is a quartic form in the spinor:*

> ds² ∼ η_μν (ψ̄γ^μψ)(ψ̄γ^νψ),   …(3.2)

*a homogeneous degree-four expression in ψ. The vector is the square root of the interval (3.1) and the spinor is the square root of the vector (3.2); hence ψ is the fourth root of the interval.*

*Proof.* Degree in ψ of V^μ ∼ ψ̄γ^μψ is 2; degree of η_μν V^μV^ν is 4. Each root halves the degree: scalar → vector (Thm 3.1) → spinor (Thm 3.2). ∎

This is the literal content of "square root of geometry," carried one level past Atiyah's slogan: the spinor is the *fourth* root of the interval. The interval is the integrated shadow (2.1) of dx₄/dt = ic; thus ψ is the fourth root of the McGucken interval. The chain is **G1**; reading the interval as the shadow of (1.1) is the standing **G2** identification.

**4. The Tensor Square of the Spinor *Is* the Exterior Algebra of the x₄-Arena**

**Theorem 4.1 (Exterior closure, 16 = 16).** *For the Dirac spinor module S of the four-dimensional arena, dim(S ⊗ S*) = 16 = dim Λ•(ℝ⁴) = Σ_{k=0}^4 C(4,k) = 1+4+6+4+1 = 16. The Fierz/Cartan basis {𝟙, γ^μ, γ^μν, γ^μνρ, γ⁵} realizes*

> S ⊗ S* ≅ Λ•(ℝ⁴_{x₄}),   …(4.1)

*with multiplicities 1, 4, 6, 4, 1 matching Λ⁰,…,Λ⁴.*

*Proof.* dim S = 4 ⇒ dim(S ⊗ S*) = 16. The sixteen Dirac bilinears form a basis of 4×4 matrices, organized by antisymmetric rank: scalar (Λ⁰), vector (Λ¹), tensor γ^μν (Λ²), axial-vector γ⁵γ^μ (Λ³), pseudoscalar γ⁵ (Λ⁴). The count 1+4+6+4+1 = 16 was verified symbolically. ∎

Geometric reading: *every* measure of the x₄-extended arena — length (vector), area (γ^μν), 3-volume, top 4-volume (γ⁵) — is a spinor bilinear. The full measure algebra of the arena is the tensor square of the spinor. Arithmetic and classification are **G1**; the arena identification is the standing **G2**. Equation (4.1) is the exact form of Atiyah's slogan in the Light Time Dimension arena.

**5. The Unique Geometric Square Root: the x₄-Stationary Null Cone**

Representation theory establishes that spinors *exist*; it does not say *what they square-root, geometrically*. Light Time Dimension supplies the referent.

**Theorem 5.1 (Geometric referent of the root).** *The object a single Weyl spinor square-roots is a null direction (Thm 3.2). In the Light Time Dimension ontology the null direction is the x₄-rest locus: the photon at dx₄/dt = 0 on its null worldline, riding the wavefront. Therefore the spinor is the square root of the dx₄/dt = 0 condition — the square root of x₄-stationarity.*

*Proof.* By 3.2, p^μ = ½ tr(σ^μ λλ†) satisfies p² = 0: p^μ lies on the null cone. By ontology (ii) the null cone is the x₄-rest locus dx₄/dt = 0. Hence λλ̄ lands on the x₄-stationary cone, and λ is its square root. ∎

This is the answer Atiyah's representation-theory complaint was missing: a geometric referent for "the half." The spinor halves the null/x₄-rest direction. The null square is **G1**; the identification null = x₄-rest, stated here as resting on ontology (ii), is *derived* in §5.2 and thereby upgraded to **G1**.

**5.2 The budget identity: the magnitude c enters here, and only here**

We isolate the single place in the entire development where the *magnitude* c — the motion itself, beyond the existence of a fourth axis — is load-bearing. Sections 3, 4, 6 and 7 require only the imaginary fourth axis (the signature, i.e. the factor i recoverable from the shadow x₄ = ict); the rate magnitude is, there, a unit convention. The exception is the identification of §5.1, which we now derive rather than assume.

**Proposition 5.2 (Four-velocity budget identity).** *From dx₄ = ic dt and the interval (2.1), a worldline of spatial speed v has proper-advance rate dτ/dt = √(1 − v²/c²). Defining the x₄-advance speed w := c (dτ/dt), the four-velocity budget is Pythagorean and saturated at c,*

> v² + w² = c²,   …(5.1)

*so the x₄-rest locus w = 0 is exactly the locus v = c.*

*Proof.* With dx₄ = ic dt, the interval (2.1) is ds² = d**x**² − c²dt² = −c²dτ², whence dτ/dt = √(1 − v²/c²). Then w² = c²(1 − v²/c²) = c² − v², so v² + w² = c² identically (verified symbolically). Setting w = 0 gives v = c. ∎

Equation (5.1) is the saturated form of "every event advances through the four-space at the single rate c": spatial motion and x₄-advance trade against a fixed budget of magnitude c. A massive particle at spatial rest (v = 0) spends the whole budget on x₄-advance (w = c); the photon (v = c) spends none (w = 0) and is at rest in x₄ — recovering canonical ontology (ii) as a *theorem* rather than a postulate. **G1.**

**Theorem 5.3 (Null cone = x₄-rest, derived — upgrade of Theorem 5.1 to G1).** *The spinor's bilinear square is null and hence sits at v = c (Thm 3.2). By Proposition 5.2 the x₄-rest locus is also v = c. Therefore the spinor's null square lies on the x₄-rest locus as a derived identity, not an assumed bridge.*

*Proof.* Immediate from Thm 3.2 (p² = 0 ⇒ v = c) and Prop 5.2 (w = 0 ⇔ v = c). ∎

This removes ontology (ii) as a standalone postulate underwriting Theorem 5.1: "null = x₄-rest" is now a consequence of the budget identity, which is a consequence of the single-c interval (2.1). The only residual input is that the interval is the one built by the expansion — the framework's definition, not an added assumption. Theorem 5.1 is thereby **G1**.

**5.3 Necessity: spinors and the x₄-expansion are one constant**

We can now state precisely, and prove, the sense in which the spinor demands that x₄ move at c.

**Theorem 5.4 (Rigidity: one constant, two faces).** *Replace the primitive by dx₄ = iu dt for a free magnitude u. Both the spinor's null cone and the x₄-rest locus then move to v = u together, since both are read from the single interval ds² = d**x**² − u²dt². Consequently:*

*(i) [Rigidity] The assignment u ↦ (spinor null structure) is injective: distinct expansion magnitudes give distinct Clifford algebras {γ^μ, γ^ν} = 2η^μν(u) and distinct null cones. Were x₄ not expanding at c, the spinor's bilinear square would lie on a different cone — the spinor would not be the object it is.*

*(ii) [Determination] The spinor's null cone is the surface on which its massless bilinear propagates, fixed empirically at the observed light speed c_obs. Equating it to the Light Time Dimension null cone v = u forces u = c_obs: the spinor's lightcone determines the expansion rate.*

*Proof.* With dx₄ = iu dt, ds² = d**x**² − u²dt²; then ds² = 0 ⇒ v = u, and Proposition 5.2 with c → u gives w = 0 ⇔ v = u. The Clifford relation depends on u through the metric, so u₁ ≠ u₂ yield inequivalent null cones (verified: cone speed equals u, injective in u); this is (i). Equating the Light Time Dimension cone v = u to the empirical massless cone v = c_obs gives u = c_obs; this is (ii). ∎ **G1.**

**Remark 5.5 (Exact scope of the necessity — what is and is not forced).** Theorem 5.4 concerns the *null/metric* structure the spinor carries, not its group-theoretic existence. The double cover, the half-angle, and the Spin module are rate-blind (§7–§8): they exist for any expansion magnitude and do not by themselves generate the expansion. What rigidly tracks c is the *location of the spinor's null cone* — the speed at which its bilinear square propagates. The formal content of "spinors demand that x₄ moves at c" is therefore exactly:

> The spinor's null cone and the x₄-expansion are a single constant entering the single interval (2.1); they cannot disagree. The empirically-fixed spinor lightcone pins the expansion magnitude to c (Thm 5.4 ii); conversely any change in the expansion relocates the spinor's null square (Thm 5.4 i).

This is a statement of *mutual determination through one constant*, and it is the strongest claim the structure supports. It is not the claim that the bare existence of spinors conjures the expansion — that would overreach the rate-blind representation theory and is explicitly not asserted.

**5.4 The signature is forced: a single-complex spinor demands one moving dimension**

Theorem 5.4 fixed the *magnitude* of the rate, given that one dimension moves. We now address the deeper question: must any dimension move at all? Given four real coordinates with no prior signature, does the spinor itself force one of them to be timelike — dx₄ = ic dt, "moving" relative to the other three — or could all four be static (a definite Euclidean metric)? The naive answer "spinors require motion" is **false**: spinors exist on the static Euclidean ℝ⁴, where Spin(4) = SU(2) × SU(2). The true statement is sharper, and concerns the *single-complex* spinor — the physical spinor carrying one complex structure i and the Hermitian (Born-probability) inner product of quantum mechanics.

**Theorem 5.6 (The signature is forced by the spinor's complex structure).** *Let S be an irreducible complex two-dimensional spinor space with a single complex structure i and Hermitian inner product ⟨·|·⟩, and reconstruct a four-vector from ψ ∈ S by V^μ = ⟨ψ|σ^μ|ψ⟩, σ^μ = (𝟙, σ_x, σ_y, σ_z). Then:*

*(i) The reconstructed four-vectors form the real four-space of Hermitian 2×2 matrices H = V⁰𝟙 + V^k σ_k, whose unique SL(2,ℂ)-invariant real quadratic form is det H = (V⁰)² − (V¹)² − (V²)² − (V³)², of Lorentzian signature (1,3). Exactly one direction is timelike.*

*(ii) The timelike direction is V⁰ = ⟨ψ|ψ⟩, the Hermitian norm — the single direction built from the complex structure i. The three spacelike directions are the traceless (Pauli) generators.*

*(iii) Written as a sum of four squares ds² = dx₁² + dx₂² + dx₃² + dx₄², the lone timelike direction must be assigned x₄ = ict (descending from the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic), so x₄² = −c²t² reproduces the (1,3) form. The i in x₄ = ict is the complex structure i of S.*

*(iv) A definite (Euclidean, fully static) four-space (4,0) cannot be realized as the Hermitian-bilinear space of a single complex spinor: the Euclidean realization is V⁰𝟙 + i V^k σ_k with det = (V⁰)² + |V⃗|², requiring an explicit i on the entire Pauli triple — three mutually anticommuting complex structures (the quaternionic structure of Spin(4) = SU(2) × SU(2)), not a single one.*

*Hence a single-complex-structure spinor demands exactly one moving dimension relative to the other three. Were all four static and on equal footing — a definite metric singling out no direction — the object would carry the quaternionic structure and would not be the single-i complex spinor. In this exact sense, if all dimensions were static the spinor would not be as it is.*

*Proof.* (i) Every Hermitian 2×2 matrix is H = V⁰𝟙 + V^k σ_k with V^μ real; det H = (V⁰)² − |V⃗|², verified symbolically. Under H ↦ AHA† with A ∈ SL(2,ℂ), det(AHA†) = |det A|² det H = det H (verified), so det is the invariant form, of signature (1,3). (ii) V⁰ = ⟨ψ|ψ⟩ = |a|² + |b|² ≥ 0 (verified), real and nonnegative; the σ_k are traceless, the V^k real; the norm requires conjugation, i.e. the complex structure. For any single spinor the invariant V·V = (V⁰)² − |V⃗|² = 0 (verified), on the null cone of the (1,3) form — consistent with Thm 3.2. (iii) x₄ = ict, descending from the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic, gives x₄² = −c²t², so dx₁²+…+dx₄² equals the (1,3) det form; the required i is the conjugation defining ⟨ψ|ψ⟩. (iv) det(V⁰𝟙 + iV^k σ_k) = (V⁰)² + |V⃗|² (verified); the definite form forces an explicit i on the Pauli triple, i.e. three anticommuting complex structures. A single complex structure yields Herm(2) and the (1,3) form, never (4,0). ∎ **G1.**

**Remark 5.7 (Exact scope, and why quantum mechanics' i is the moving dimension).** The theorem does not claim spinors cannot exist without motion — Euclidean Spin(4) spinors exist. It claims that the *single-complex* spinor, the one carrying exactly one imaginary unit and the Hermitian inner product quantum mechanics actually uses, has a natural four-space of signature (1,3) with exactly one timelike direction, and that this direction is the norm direction built from that very i. The complex structure of the spinor and the moving dimension are therefore the *same* i: the i of the wavefunction's ⟨ψ|ψ⟩ is the i of x₄ = ict. This is the structural root of Proposition 6.1 and the i-insertion correspondence — the single i that builds the spinor's phase, the Born norm, and the fourth axis is one object. A fully static four-space would be the quaternionic (SU(2) × SU(2)) world, in which the single i of quantum mechanics is replaced by an anticommuting triple; the complex spinor, the Born norm, and the moving fourth dimension would all be absent together. The necessity is thus not "motion or no spinor," but the tighter "one i, one moving dimension — or neither."

(γ^μ p_μ)² = (g^{μν}p_μ p_ν) 𝟙, (5.1)

**Theorem 5.3 (Quartic interval: the spinor is the fourth root of the McGucken interval).** *Composing Theorems 5.1 and 5.2, the interval is a quartic form in the spinor,*

ds² ∼g_{μν} (ψ̄γ^μψ)(ψ̄γ^νψ), (5.3)

*homogeneous of degree four in ψ. The vector is the square root of the interval (5.1) and the spinor the square root of the vector (5.2); hence ψ is the fourth root of the interval, which by Theorem 2.1 is the mere integrated shadow of dx₄/dt = ic.*

This is the Fierz classification [21], here proved on the page. ∎ **G1.** Every measure of the four-dimensional arena — length, area, 3-volume, 4-volume — is a spinor bilinear.

By Theorem 2.3 the locus v_{x₄} = 0 is also v = c. Therefore the spinor square-roots the locus of absolute rest in x₄: the null generators of Σ⁺(p), which the McGucken Spheres sweep out.*

*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of x₄ at c, dx₄/dt = ic. Direct from Theorems 5.2 and 2.3. ∎ **G1.** The geometric referent of "the half" is the null direction, which the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework identifies with absolute rest in x₄ by the budget identity, a theorem (2.3).

**Theorem 5.6 (Rigidity: one constant, two faces).** *Replace the Principle by dx₄ = iu dt with a free magnitude u. The Clifford relation depends on u through g, so u₁ ≠u₂ give inequivalent cones. ∎ **G1.** The double cover, half-angle, and spin module of Sections 6–7 are rate-blind; what tracks c is the location of the spinor's null cone. **6. The Two Mysteries Are One: √−1 and the Spinor**

**Proposition 6.1 (Identity of the mysteries).** *The geometric meaning of √−1 and the geometric meaning of the spinor are the same content, because both are built from the single i of dx₄/dt = ic.*

*Argument.* (a) Multiplication by i is the quarter-turn of the plane; dx₄/dt = ic states the x₄-rate is c rotated 90° out of real coordinate time. The x₄ axis *is* the geometric meaning of √−1 — the physical fourth axis, not an abstract Argand plane. (b) The spinor rotation operator U(θ) = exp(−i θ/2 σ·n̂) = cos(θ/2) 𝟙 − i sin(θ/2)(σ·n̂) carries its half-angle phase by the *same* imaginary unit; by the i-insertion correspondence the i making the rotation unitary is one insertion case among the twelve, the x₄ signature. (c) Therefore both of Atiyah's mysterious objects are the one i that defines x₄: √−1 *is* the x₄ axis, and the spinor's half-angle runs on that axis. They were never two puzzles. ∎

**9.1 The conjugation square is the bilinear square**

We use the quaternion realization of the transport: unit elements q = a 𝟙 + b⃗·J⃗ with J_k = −iσ_k obeying J_a J_b = −δ_ab 𝟙 + ε_abc J_c, parametrizing S³ = {a² + |b⃗|² = 1} ⊂ ℝ⁴. The scalar a is the x₄-aligned component of Theorem 5.6; the triple b⃗ spans observable 3-space (the traceless part).

**Lemma 9.1 (Conjugation angle-doubling).** *Let q(α) = cos α 𝟙 + sin α (n̂·J⃗), a point of S³ with scalar part cos α. The conjugation action v ↦ q v q⁻¹ on the traceless (3-space) part is the rotation by angle 2α about n̂. The transport q turns by the half-angle α; observable 3-space registers 2α.*

*Proof.* For n̂ = ẑ, direct computation gives q v q⁻¹: (x,y,z) ↦ (x cos2α − y sin2α, x sin2α + y cos2α, z), verified symbolically (the difference from the rotation-by-2α matrix is identically zero). General n̂ follows by spatial covariance. ∎ **G1.**

The fibre over each rotation is {±q} — exactly the square-root sign ambiguity. The transport group is S³, double-covering SO(3) = S³/{±𝟙} = ℝP³. **V.1 Spatial Rotations on Matter**

Consider a spatial rotation in the (x₁, x₂) plane by angle θ. The generator is the bivector e₁₂, and the rotation acts on a matter field ψ by:


ψ →exp(θ /2 ·e₁₂) ψ = [cos(θ /2) + sin(θ /2) ·e₁₂] ψ


using e₁₂² = −1 — which descends from the Clifford structure of the Minkowski metric of the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic (III.2) — to evaluate the exponential, with e₁₂ playing the role of i.

At θ = 2π:


ψ →[cos(π) + sin(π) ·e₁₂] ψ = -ψ


A full spatial rotation by 2π flips the sign of the matter field. Only at θ = 4π does the field return to itself.

**V.2 The Double Cover**

The map from rotation angle θ to matter-field transformation is therefore:

- θ ∈ [0, 4π) ↔ spinor transformation
- θ ∈ [0, 2π) ↔ vector rotation

Two distinct spinor transformations (at θ and θ + 2π) correspond to the same vector rotation. This is the SU(2) → SO(3) double cover, derived geometrically from the single-sided bivector action on x₄-oriented matter — where “single-sided” now has the rigorous meaning established in Theorem IV.3.

**V.3 The Pauli Matrices**

For spatial rotations, the three bivectors e₁₂, e₂₃, e₃₁ — the spatial-rotation generators of the Clifford algebra of the metric of the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic — generate the rotation subalgebra acting on the McGucken-Sphere standing wave. Their products and commutators reproduce the quaternion algebra:

e₁₂ ·e₂₃ = e₁₃ (up to sign from the Clifford product) [e₁₂, e₂₃] = 2 e₁₃ (with appropriate signs)

In the minimal complex representation, using the convention fixed in II.4:

e₂₃ ↔ -iσ₁, e₃₁ ↔ -iσ₂, e₁₂ ↔ -iσ₃

The spinor transformation under a rotation by θ about the n̂ axis becomes:

ψ →exp(-iθ /2 ·n̂·σ) ψ

which is the standard SU(2) rotation operator for spin-½ (the overall sign is a convention; the physical content is the half-angle). The spin-½ representation is forced by the half-angle, which is forced by the single-sided action, which is forced by the theorem of IV.3 — which is ultimately forced by matter’s x₄-orientation constraint (M).

**5 The Twelve Factor-of-i Insertions: A Unified Geometric Origin**
The imaginary unit appears across twelve distinct points in quantum theory, each introduced historically by hand for a locally motivated reason \[10, 11, 12, 22, 23\], each justified operationally by its necessity for agreement with experiment. The McGucken Principle identifies all twelve as instances of a single geometric fact \[30, 33, 44, 27\]: each is a projection onto the x₄ axis, and the factor of i is the algebraic record of that projection. Before addressing the twelve cases individually, we establish a structural lemma that underlies every proof.

**Lemma 14** (The suppression map σ). *Let M be the four-dimensional real Euclidean manifold with coordinates (x1,x2,x3,x4) \[46\]. The suppression map σ:M→M3,t sends (x1,x2,x3,x4) to (x1,x2,x3,t) where t=x4/(ic)=−ix4/c. Under σ, any differential operator on M involving ∂/∂x4 is transformed by the chain rule:∂∂x4=∂t∂x4⋅∂∂t=1ic⋅∂∂t=−ic⋅∂∂t,∂∂t=ic⋅∂∂x4.Any geometric object on M defined via ∂/∂x4 acquires, when transported through σ, an explicit factor of i proportional to its x4-derivative order.*

*Proof.* Direct chain rule application using t = - ix₄/c. ◻

**Remark 15**. Lemma 14 performs the heavy lifting for every case below. When an expression on M involves n factors of ∂/∂x₄, its image under σ acquires n factors of i (with factors of c absorbed into scale). The i in the quantum expression is the count of x₄-derivatives in the underlying geometric object on M. This is what “projection onto x₄” means algebraically: the i is not a formal ornament; it is a bookkeeping device recording how many times x₄ appears in the real construction. The chain-rule operator ∂/∂t = ic ∂/∂x₄ is the McGucken Operator D_M = ∂ₜ + ic ∂_{x₄} \[34\], the directional derivative along the integral curves of dx₄/dt = ic, which co-generates with the McGucken hypersurface the source-pair ( ℳ_G,D_M ) that simultaneously exalts arena, structure, operator, and dynamics from the single source-relation dx₄/dt = ic.

**Theorem 16** (Unified geometric origin of the twelve i insertions). *Under the McGucken Principle \[30, 33, 44, 27\], the imaginary unit i appearing in each of the following twelve canonical expressions of quantum theory is the algebraic marker of projection onto the x4 axis:*

1.  *Canonical quantization: p̂→−iℏ∂/∂x, Ê→iℏ∂/∂t.*
2.  *Schrödinger equation: iℏ∂ψ/∂t=Ĥψ.*
3.  *Canonical commutator: \[q̂,p̂\]=iℏ.*
4.  *Dirac equation: (iγμ∂μ−m)ψ=0.*
5.  *Path integral weight: eiS/ℏ.*
6.  *Propagator regularization: +iε prescription.*
7.  *Wick substitution: t→−iτ.*
8.  *Fresnel integrals: i factors in semiclassical approximation.*
9.  *Minkowski–Euclidean bridge: iSM=−SE.*
10. *U(1) gauge phase: eiθ in electromagnetic gauge theory.*
11. *Spinor structure: imaginary structure of Dirac spinor representations and the SU(2) double cover.*
12. *KMS condition: imaginary-time periodicity ℏβ in thermal field theory.*

*In each case, the i is the σ-image of a real geometric structure on M.*

*Proof.* We establish the identification in each of the twelve cases.

**(i) Canonical quantization.** The four-momentum on M is P_μ = ħk_μ with k_μ the real four-wavevector dual to ( x₁,x₂,x₃,x₄ ). The momentum operator on M is {P̂}_μ = - iħ ∂/∂x_μ in the convention where wavefunctions on M have the form e^{ik ·x}. The x₄-component is {P̂}₄ = - iħ ∂/∂x₄. Applying Lemma 14: {P̂}₄ = - iħ·( - i/c) ·∂/∂t = - (ħ/c) ∂/∂t. The relation Ê = c{P̂}₄ (consistent with x₄ = ict and the ( - , + , + , + ) signature) requires positive-energy solutions ψ ∼e^{- iEt/ħ}, forcing Ê = iħ ∂/∂t. The i is the σ chain-rule factor.

**(ii) Schrödinger equation.** A wavefunction ψ on M for a non-relativistic massive particle satisfies a first-order x₄-evolution equation - ħc ∂φ/∂x₄ = {Ĥ}_{nonrel}φ, real on M. Applying Lemma 14: - ħc ·∂φ/∂x₄ = - ħc ·( - i/c) ·∂φ/∂t = iħ ∂φ/∂t. The equation becomes iħ ∂φ/∂t = Ĥφ. Schrödinger’s 1926 insertion of the i by hand was the insertion required to match this chain-rule factor.

**(iii) Canonical commutator.** On M, the commutator [{q̂}ᵢ,∂/∂xⱼ ]= δᵢⱼ is a real identity. The momentum operator acquires its i from the wavefunction ansatz ψ ∼e^{ip ·x/ħ} inherited from x₄-projection (case (i)). Therefore [q̂,p̂ ]= [q̂, - iħ ∂/∂x ]= iħ. The i is the same σ chain-rule factor propagated through the momentum operator. (A complete dual-channel derivation of this commutator from dx₄/dt = ic is given in Theorem 30 below.)

**(iv) Dirac equation.** On M, the Dirac equation is ( γ_E^μ∂_μ + m )ψ = 0 with Euclidean gamma matrices satisfying {γ_E^μ,γ_E^ν} = 2δ^{μν}. This is a real first-order equation with no i. Under σ, γ_E⁴ becomes iγ_M⁰ (because γ_E⁴ squares to + 1 on M, but its σ-image must square to - 1 in Minkowski signature, achieved by the factor i); the chain rule contributes another i via ∂/∂x₄ = - (i/c) ∂/∂t. Combined, γ_E⁴ ∂/∂x₄ becomes iγ_M⁰ ·( - i/c) ·∂/∂t = (1/c)γ_M⁰ ∂/∂t, with cancellation; the remaining global i in the Minkowski Dirac equation absorbs the overall sign required for Hermiticity. The i is the joint signature-change-and-chain-rule image of the real Euclidean Dirac operator.

**(v) Path integral weight.** The Euclidean path integral weight on M is e^{- S_E/ħ} with S_E a real positive-definite functional. By Theorem 9, iS_M = - S_E, so e^{- S_E/ħ} = e^{iS_M/ħ}. The i in e^{iS_M/ħ} is the algebraic result of transforming the real Euclidean weight through σ. Feynman’s 1948 insertion was required because he was computing in t-coordinates and needed the factor that σ supplies.

**(vi) +iε prescription.** On M, propagators are 1/( k² + m² ) with k² = k₁² + k₂² + k₃² + k₄² ≥ 0 > - m², well-defined everywhere. Under σ, k₄ becomes - iω/c, producing the Minkowski k² = |k|² - ω²/c² with mixed signature, which vanishes on the light cone. The + iε prescription tilts the contour infinitesimally toward x₄ via k₄→k₄ + iε/c, the partial-σ image of real-axis regularization on M. Proved formally as Theorem 12.

**(vii) Wick substitution.** Proved as Theorem 6: t→- iτ is the coordinate identification τ = x₄/c. The i is the σ chain-rule factor for the full coordinate change.

**(viii) Fresnel integrals.** Gaussian integrals on M have the form ∫e^{- as²}ds = √{π/a} for real positive a, no phase. Under partial σ rotating the integration contour by angle θ, the integral acquires a phase e^{- iθ}. At θ = π/4 (half-Wick), Gaussian integrals with imaginary quadratic phase ∫e^{ias²}ds acquire √{π/(ia)} = √{π/a} ·e^{- iπ/4}. The √{i} in Fresnel integrals is the σ-image at half-Wick angle.

**(ix) Minkowski–Euclidean bridge.** Proved as Theorem 9: iS_M = - S_E via the chain-rule factor dt = - i dτ.

**(x) U(1) gauge phase.** On M, electromagnetism is the gauge theory of local x₄-phase invariance. A complex scalar ψ invariant under ψ→e^αψ (real α) corresponds to a real exponential profile ψ ∼e^{k₄x₄} along x₄. Under σ, e^{k₄x₄} becomes e^{iω t} with ω = k₄c. The gauge transformation ψ→e^αψ on M becomes ψ→e^{iα}ψ in Minkowski coordinates with the i pulled in from σ. The i in e^{iθ} of U(1) gauge theory is the σ-image of the real exponential phase on M.

**(xi) Spinor structure and the SU(2) double cover.** Spin representations of SO(4) on M are real: {Spin}(4) = SU(2) ×SU(2) with real double-cover structure. Under σ, the signature change from Euclidean SO(4) to Lorentzian SO(3,1) corresponds to analytic continuation of one SU(2) factor into SL(2,{ℂ}), with γ_E⁴→iγ_M⁰ and half-angle rotations in ( x₀,x₄ ) becoming complex boosts. The i in Dirac spinor representations is the σ-image of the real spin structure on M. The 4π fermion periodicity is the geometric signature of rotation in a real x₄ axis advancing at ic: a rotation about a spatial direction in the ( xᵢ,x₄ ) plane requires 4π to return the spinor to its original orientation precisely because x₄ is itself advancing during the rotation.

**(xii) KMS condition.** Periodic identification of the x₄ axis with period L₄ produces a compact circle in x₄, corresponding by Matsubara mode analysis to thermal equilibrium at T = ħc/( k_BL₄ ). Under σ, x₄-periodicity with period L₄ = ħβ c becomes t-periodicity with period ħβ in imaginary time. The KMS condition ⟨A(t)B(0)⟩= ⟨B(0)A(t + iħβ)⟩ expresses this x₄-periodicity in t-coordinates. The i is the σ-image of real x₄-periodicity on M. ◻

**Theorem 17** (Meta-theorem: classification of the unified i). *In all twelve cases of Theorem 16, the factor of i appearing in the standard quantum-theoretic expression is the σ-image of a real geometric object on M. The i arises through one of three mechanisms:*

1.  *Chain-rule factor. The substitution ∂/∂t=ic∂/∂x4 produces one factor of i per x4-derivative. Cases (i), (ii), (iii), (v), (ix), (xii).*
2.  *Signature-change factor. Tensor structures (gamma matrices, spin structures) acquire i to match the Minkowski signature under σ. Cases (iv), (xi).*
3.  *Image of integration-contour or exponential structures. Real objects on M become imaginary-phase objects in t-coordinates. Cases (vi), (vii), (viii), (x).*

*Every factor of i in quantum theory falls into one of these three mechanisms. There is no instance where i appears without a corresponding x4-projection structure on M to explain it.*

*Proof.* Theorem 16 established each case individually. Inspection of the twelve proofs shows that each falls into exactly one of the three mechanisms (a), (b), (c). Completeness of the classification — that every i in quantum theory falls into one of the three — is the content of the case-by-case proof of Theorem 16. ◻

**Remark 18**. Theorem 17 consolidates the twelve case-by-case proofs into a structural claim: every i in quantum theory is a record of how many times x₄ appears in the underlying real construction on M, translated through σ into t-coordinates. The century-long accumulation of “i by hand” insertions — each historically justified by a different local physical requirement — is revealed as the systematic appearance of σ-chain-rule factors, σ-signature-change factors, and σ-images of real structures, all traceable to the single geometric fact that x₄ is a real axis advancing at ic. No physical Principle independent of the McGucken Principle is required to explain the presence of i anywhere in quantum theory.

# 7. The x₄-Orientation of Matter and the Single-Sided Action: The Corrected Theorem

The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension x₄ is expanding at the velocity of light: dx₄/dt = ic, with x₄ = ict, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action h and whose volume defines a nonlocality.

*In the author's words — reproduced verbatim and in full from [5], §III.1, §III.2, §III.3, §III.4, §IV.1, §IV.2, §IV.3, §IV.4, §IV.5, §IV.6 (the Dirac paper; verified-read). Equation and reference numbers are those of [5].*

**III.1 Bivectors as Oriented Plane Elements**

A bivector is an oriented plane element, the 4D analog of an oriented area in 2D or volume in 3D. In the 4D Clifford algebra, bivectors are the grade-2 elements — antisymmetric products of two vectors:


e_{ab} = eₐ ∧e_b = 1/2(eₐ e_b - e_b eₐ)


There are six independent bivectors in 4D, corresponding to the six independent planes:

- Spatial bivectors (purely real): e₁₂, e₂₃, e₃₁
- x₄-involving bivectors (carrying the i of x₄): e₁₄, e₂₄, e₃₄

**III.2 The Squaring Behavior**

The square of a bivector is determined by the Clifford algebra. For a purely spatial bivector:


e₁₂² = e₁e₂e₁e₂ = -e₁e₁e₂e₂ = -(+1)(+1) = -1


using {e₁, e₂} = 0 and eᵢ² = +1 for spatial basis vectors. Spatial bivectors square to −1; they are the geometric analogs of imaginary units, and they generate compact rotations.

For an x₄-involving bivector:


e₁₄² = e₁e₄e₁e₄ = -e₁e₁e₄e₄ = -(+1)(-1) = +1


using e₄² = η₄₄ = −1 from the Lorentzian signature. x₄-involving bivectors square to +1; they generate non-compact boosts.

This compact/non-compact split is the geometric origin of the difference between rotations (periodic) and boosts (unbounded rapidity). It traces directly to the i in dx₄/dt = ic via the signature of η₄₄.

**III.3 Bivectors as Rotation Generators**

A rotation in the plane of a bivector P by angle θ is generated by exponentiation:


R(θ) = exp(θ /2 ·e_P)


The factor of 1/2 is the subject of Sections IV and V. It is not imposed — it emerges from the geometry of how matter couples to bivectors via the x₄-expansion.

**III.4 The Pseudoscalar**

A key object in what follows is the Clifford pseudoscalar:


I = γ⁰γ¹γ²γ³


This is the unit 4-volume element. Direct computation using the Clifford algebra shows:

- I² = −1
- I anticommutes with every vector γᵘ
- I commutes with every bivector γᵘγᵛ (μ ≠ ν)

The pseudoscalar serves as a natural “i” for the 4D Clifford algebra. In Light, Time, Dimension Theory, this I is the geometric embodiment of the i in the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic. The i appearing in matter field phases e^(ikx₄) is I in disguise; when we write the Dirac equation in full Clifford-algebraic form, the complex structure of quantum mechanics emerges as the pseudoscalar structure of 4D spacetime.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**IV.1 Motivation from the Standing-Wave Structure**

Matter, as established in II.2, is an x₄-standing wave with phase accumulating in the direction of increasing x₄. This gives matter an intrinsic orientation relative to the x₄-axis: the wavefunction phase evolves as e^(+ikx₄) with k > 0 for ordinary matter. In the Clifford-algebraic formulation, where the pseudoscalar I plays the role of the imaginary unit i, this becomes:


Ψ_{matter}(x, x₄) = Ψ₀(x) ·exp(I ·kx₄)


The previous version of this paper described matter’s “x₄-orientation” using pictorial language of leading and trailing edges. That description was geometrically suggestive but not mathematically precise, and a hostile referee would correctly object that left-multiplication and right-multiplication in a Clifford algebra do not literally act on different “sides” of a physical object — both are operations performed at the same spacetime point on the same multivector. We now give the rigorous formulation.

**IV.2 The Matter Orientation Constraint**

**Definition (matter orientation condition).** An even-grade multivector Ψ in Cl(1,3) is said to carry matter x₄-orientation at Compton frequency k > 0 if there exists an even-grade multivector Ψ₀ — the rest-frame amplitude — and a real scalar x₄ such that:

Ψ(x, x₄) = Ψ₀(x) ·exp(+I ·kx₄), k > 0     (M)

with multiplication performed on the right. The corresponding condition for antimatter is Ψ(x, x₄) = Ψ₀(x) · exp(−I · kx₄). Here k = mc/ℏ is the x₄-wavevector of the McGucken-Principle wavefront: the Compton frequency of II.2, the rate at which dx₄/dt = ic advances the phase of a rest-mass-m standing wave. The whole content of (M) descends from the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic — the x₄-rotor exp(I · kx₄) is the phase the spherically symmetric wavefront accumulates, and the pseudoscalar I is the geometric embodiment of the i in dx₄/dt = ic (III.4).

This is an algebraic constraint on Ψ, not a pictorial one. It specifies a definite relationship between the x₄-dependence of the multivector and its rest-frame value, via right-multiplication by the x₄-rotor. The key features of (M) are:

1. The sign of k is positive — this is what distinguishes matter from antimatter.
2. The x₄-dependence enters through right-multiplication — this is what picks out a preferred side of the bivector action on Ψ.
3. The pseudoscalar I, not an abstract imaginary unit, is the generator — this ties the phase structure to the 4D Clifford geometry.

**IV.3 Theorem: Single-Sided Action Preserves the Matter Constraint**

**Theorem (single-sided preservation).** Let R = exp(θ/2 · e_P) be a rotor generated by a spatial bivector e_P (i.e., e_P ∈ {e₁₂, e₂₃, e₃₁}). Let Ψ satisfy the matter orientation condition (M). Then:

\(a\) Left-action Ψ → RΨ preserves (M): RΨ satisfies (M) with rest-frame amplitude Ψ₀’ = RΨ₀ and the same Compton frequency k.

\(b\) Sandwich action Ψ → R⁻¹ΨR does *not* preserve (M) in general: R⁻¹ΨR fails to admit a decomposition of the form Ψ₀” · exp(+I · kx₄) for any rest-frame amplitude Ψ₀” and the original k > 0.

**Proof.**

*Part (a).* Let R be independent of x₄ (spatial bivectors commute with x₄, so R depends only on spatial coordinates or is constant). Then:

RΨ = R · Ψ₀ · exp(+I · kx₄) = (RΨ₀) · exp(+I · kx₄)

which satisfies (M) with Ψ₀’ = RΨ₀. The positive k is preserved.

*Part (b).* Compute the sandwich action:


R⁻¹Ψ R = R⁻¹ ·Ψ₀ ·exp(+I ·kx₄) ·R


We use two key facts about the spatial bivector e_P: (i) Spatial bivectors commute with the pseudoscalar I (since I = γ⁰γ¹γ²γ³ and spatial bivectors involve only spatial γ’s, the commutator [e_P, I] = 0 follows by direct computation using the Clifford algebra). (ii) Therefore R commutes with exp(+I · kx₄).

Using (ii):


R⁻¹ ·Ψ₀ ·exp(+I ·kx₄) ·R = R⁻¹ ·Ψ₀ ·R ·exp(+I ·kx₄)


So the sandwich action on Ψ is equivalent to the sandwich action on Ψ₀, leaving the x₄-rotor intact. Superficially this might seem to preserve (M). But now consider the general case where R is extended to an x₄-involving bivector — say R = exp(φ/2 · e_₁₄). Now R does *not* commute with I, because x₄-involving bivectors anticommute with the spatial γ’s they do not contain, and one computes:

[e₁₄, I] = 2 e₁₄ · I_⊥ ≠ 0 (where I_⊥ denotes the pseudoscalar projected onto the bivector’s orthogonal complement)

The sandwich action then produces:


R⁻¹ ·Ψ₀ ·exp(+I ·kx₄) ·R = R⁻¹ ·Ψ₀ ·R ·exp(+R⁻¹ ·I ·R ·kx₄)


and R⁻¹ · I · R ≠ I in general for x₄-involving R. The exponent is therefore not the same pseudoscalar I appearing in (M), and the resulting multivector fails to satisfy the matter orientation condition with the original I.

The critical observation: the sandwich action for the x₄-involving bivector generates a transformed pseudoscalar R⁻¹IR, which by direct computation has a component along the negative-I direction. The right-multiplication by R thus partially converts exp(+I · kx₄) into a mixture containing exp(−I · kx₄) — that is, it partially converts matter into antimatter. This is the precise algebraic content of the earlier pictorial statement that “the right-action would attempt to rotate the x₄-orientation backwards.” ∎

**IV.4 What the Theorem Establishes**

The theorem replaces the pictorial “leading edge / trailing edge” argument with a concrete algebraic fact: the sandwich action, applied to an x₄-oriented matter field, produces a multivector that no longer satisfies the matter orientation condition. In particular, for bivectors involving x₄, the sandwich action introduces an antimatter component. Only left-action (single-sided transformation) preserves the matter constraint across the full group of bivector generators needed to describe all Lorentz transformations.

Consequently, matter fields must transform under bivector generators by single-sided action only:

Ψ →exp(θ /2 ·e_P) Ψ

The half-angle in the spinor rotation is the theorem that single-sided transformation is the unique action on matter fields preserving the x₄-orientation constraint (M) across all bivector generators.

**IV.5 Why Vectors See the Full Angle**

To solidify the contrast: a 4-vector like dxᵘ does not satisfy the matter orientation condition (M). It has no x₄-phase structure, no exp(+I · kx₄) factor, no preferred sign of k. The matter constraint simply does not apply to vectors. For vectors, the geometrically natural transformation is the sandwich action R⁻¹vR, which preserves the vector’s grade (a vector stays a vector) and rotates it by angle θ. There is no asymmetry to break because there is no oriented phase structure to preserve.

Matter, being defined by (M), is in a different algebraic class. Its defining constraint picks out right-multiplication as the locus of x₄-orientation, and the theorem of IV.3 then forces single-sided transformation as the unique orientation-preserving action.

**IV.6 A Variational Perspective**

The same conclusion can be reached from an action-principle argument, which we sketch here for completeness. The action is not imported from outside: in the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic the phase the wavefront accumulates is the action in units of ℏ (II.5, Step 3), and least action is itself a McGucken-derived result — the stationary-phase condition on the McGucken-Sphere superposition. The rest-frame Lagrangian for a field with the x₄-oriented phase structure of (M) is proportional to:

L_{rest} ∝ Ψ̄ (i γ^u ∂_μ - m) Ψ

where Ψ̄ = Ψ† γ⁰ is the Dirac adjoint. Under a left-action Ψ → RΨ (with R an even-grade rotor, R† = R⁻¹ for spatial bivectors), the adjoint transforms as Ψ̄ → Ψ̄ R⁻¹, and the bilinear Ψ̄(…)Ψ is invariant precisely when the operator (i γᵘ ∂_μ − m) commutes with R — which holds for spatial rotations. Under a sandwich action Ψ → R⁻¹ΨR, the bilinear Ψ̄(…)Ψ becomes R⁻¹ Ψ̄ (…) Ψ R, which is not a scalar: it picks up grade-2 and grade-4 components that the original action did not contain. The sandwich action thus produces a non-scalar Lagrangian, which is not an admissible transformation of the action.

Single-sided action is therefore both the unique transformation preserving the matter orientation constraint (M) algebraically (Theorem IV.3) and the unique transformation preserving the scalar character of the Dirac Lagrangian (variational argument). Both routes close the gap in the previous version’s argument.

The matter field is written in the spacetime algebra of Hestenes [18, 19] and Doran–Lasenby [17]: a Dirac spinor is an even-grade multivector Ψ ∈Cl⁺(1,3), eight real dimensions spanned by 𝟙, the six bivectors, and I, and the column spinor is recovered by the correspondence ψ = Ψ ξ₀ with ξ₀ a fixed reference spinor (Section 10).

**Definition 7.1 (Matter orientation condition (M)).** Let B ≡γ²γ¹, a spatial bivector with B² = -𝟙 (Theorem 4.4). An even-grade multivector Ψ carries matter x₄-orientation at Compton frequency ω_C = mc²/ħ> 0 if there is an even-grade rest amplitude Ψ₀(x) with

With t = x₄/(ic) the same rotor reads exp(iB k x₄), k = mc/ħ, so the phase is the wavefront's x₄-advance sampled at the Compton wavelength.

**Theorem 7.2 (Left action preserves (M) for every rotor; right action preserves (M) exactly on the commutant of the phase bivector; the timelike bivector reverses the phase).** *Let L be any rotor of the even subalgebra (any element of Spin⁺(1,3)). Then:*

*(c) For the timelike bivector T ≡γ⁰γ¹, TB = -BT, hence T⁻¹BT = -B and*

Ψ₀ exp(-Bω_C t) T = (Ψ₀ T) exp(+Bω_C t): (7.1)

*right multiplication by a bivector containing the x₄ direction converts a field satisfying (M) with +ω_C into one satisfying (M) with -ω_C — matter into antimatter.*

*Consequently the Lorentz group must act on matter fields by single-sided left multiplication: of the two sides, left multiplication is the one that preserves (M) for every rotor, while the right side is reserved for the Compton phase and for the x₄-orientation reversal of (7.1).*

*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of x₄ at c, dx₄/dt = ic. (a) LΨ₀exp(-Bω_C t) = (LΨ₀)exp(-Bω_C t) by associativity. (c) T² = +𝟙 (Theorem 4.4), so T⁻¹ = T, and T⁻¹BT = -B; substituting into (b)'s identity gives (7.1). ∎ **G1.**

**Theorem 7.3 (The half-angle and the SU(2) double cover on matter).** *Under a spatial rotation by θ in the (1,2) plane, matter transforms by the left action Ψ ↦exp((θ)/2γ¹γ²)Ψ of Theorem 7.2(a), so that Ψ ↦-Ψ at θ = 2π and Ψ ↦Ψ only at θ = 4π (Theorem 6.3), while a vector v, which does not satisfy (M), transforms by the sandwich v ↦RvR⁻¹ through the full angle (6.1). **Remark 7.4 (Correction to [5], §IV.3).** The source paper states in its §III.4 that "I commutes with every bivector γᵘγᵛ (μ ≠ ν)" and in its §IV.3(b) that for an x₄-involving bivector "R does *not* commute with I … [e₁₄, I] = 2 e₁₄ · I_⊥ ≠ 0". The conclusion of [5] (single-sided left action, the half-angle, right multiplication by the timelike bivector as x₄-reversal) is unchanged; its proof is replaced by Theorem 7.2.

**Theorem 7.5 (Variational form).** *The Dirac Lagrangian density ℒ = ψ̄(iγ^μ∂_μ - mc/ħ)ψ, ψ̄ = ψ^†γ⁰, is invariant under the left action ψ ↦Sψ, ψ̄ ↦ψ̄ S⁻¹ with S in the spinor representation of SO⁺(1,3) and S⁻¹γ^μ S = Λ^μ{}_νγ^ν. **1. Foundational Postulate**
**Postulate 1: The McGucken Principle**
The fourth dimension expands spherically at the invariant speed of light:


(dx₄)/(dt) = ic.


Here x₄ = ict, and the imaginary unit i records the perpendicularity of the fourth coordinate to the ordinary spatial coordinates x₁,x₂,x₃. The McGucken quantum-mechanics paper treats this postulate as the origin of complex quantum phase, the wavefunction, the Born rule, nonlocality, and the Feynman apparatus [1].

**Theorem 1: x₄ = ict Generates the Minkowski Metric**
The substitution x₄ = ict transforms the Euclidean four-coordinate line element into the Minkowski line element.

**Proof**
Begin with the four-coordinate expression


ds_E² = dx₁² + dx₂² + dx₃² + dx₄².


Using x₄ = ict,


dx₄² = (icdt)² = - c²dt².


Therefore


ds_E² = dx₁² + dx₂² + dx₃² - c²dt².


This is the Minkowski interval in mostly-plus convention. Hence the Lorentzian signature is generated by the perpendicular fourth-dimensional coordinate x₄ = ict. □

**Theorem 2: The McGucken Sphere Is the Future Null Cone and the Foundational Atom of Spacetime**
The spherical expansion of x₄ at speed c projects into ordinary spacetime as the future null cone


Σ₊(p) = { x:(x - p)² = 0,x⁰ > p⁰}.


This null sphere is the foundational atom of spacetime: the primitive causal-incidence unit from which local metric structure, null propagation, twistor incidence, and positive scattering geometry are successively generated.

**Proof**
Set ds² = 0 in the line element derived above:


dx₁² + dx₂² + dx₃² - c²dt² = 0.


Therefore


|x - x₀|² = c²(t - t₀)².


For t > t₀, this is a spatial sphere of radius c(t - t₀). In spacetime, the union of these expanding spheres is the future null cone of p = (t₀,x₀). This is the McGucken Sphere Σ₊(p). Because Σ₊(p) is generated at each event and supplies the primitive null-incidence relation for all later constructions, it is the foundational atom of spacetime in the present theory. □

**Plain-language meaning**
The McGucken Sphere is simply the light cone seen as a real expanding sphere produced by the fourth dimension. Instead of treating the light cone as a kinematic constraint, this framework treats it as the projection of x₄-expansion. This is why the McGucken sphere is called the foundational atom of spacetime: every event contributes one such primitive expanding null unit, and the relations among these units generate causal, quantum, twistor, and amplituhedral structure.

**4. Penrose Twistor Space from McGucken Incidence**
**Definition 1: McGucken Twistor**
A McGucken twistor is a projective spinor pair


Z^α = (ω^A,π_{A^′})


with incidence relation


ω^A = ix^{AA^′}π_{A^′}.


The McGucken twistor paper identifies this relation as the physical origin of Penrose twistor incidence, with i inherited from x₄ = ict [3].

**Theorem 6: McGucken Sphere Incidence Generates CP³**
For each spacetime point x, the null directions of the McGucken Sphere define a CP¹ line in projective twistor space; the union of these incidence lines generates CP³.

**Proof**
At fixed x, a null direction is represented by a nonzero spinor π_{A^′}, modulo projective rescaling:


π_{A^′} ∼rπ_{A^′}, r ∈ℂ*.


The space of such directions is CP¹. For each π_{A^′}, define


ω^A = ix^{AA^′}π_{A^′}.


Then


Z^α = (ω^A,π_{A^′})


is a point of CP³, and the set of all such Z^α for fixed x forms a projective line CP¹. Varying x sweeps out projective twistor space. Therefore CP³ is the projectivized incidence geometry of McGucken null spheres. □

**Theorem 7: Null Rays Correspond to Twistor Points**
A null generator of a McGucken Sphere corresponds to a point in projective twistor space.

**Proof**
A null generator is specified by x and projective spinor π_{A^′}. Incidence gives


Z^α = (ix^{AA^′}π_{A^′},π_{A^′}).


Rescaling π_{A^′}↦rπ_{A^′} rescales Z^α↦rZ^α, leaving the projective twistor point unchanged. Therefore each null generator defines one projective twistor point. □

**Plain-language meaning**
An event emits a sphere of null directions. Projectivize those directions and the event becomes a CP¹ line in twistor space. This gives a direct physical reading of Penrose’s point-line correspondence.

# 9. The Dirac Equation

The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension x₄ is expanding at the velocity of light: dx₄/dt = ic, with x₄ = ict, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action h and whose volume defines a nonlocality.

*In the author's words — reproduced verbatim and in full from [5], §VI.1, §VI.2, §VI.3, §IX.1, §IX.2 (the Dirac paper; verified-read). Equation and reference numbers are those of [5].*

**VI.1 Weyl Chiralities from x₄-Orientation**

Matter has two possible x₄-orientations: forward (exp(+I · kx₄)) and its mirror (exp(−I · kx₄)). These correspond to the two Weyl chiralities — left-handed and right-handed spinors. Formally, defining the chirality projectors P_L = ½(1 − γ⁵) and P_R = ½(1 + γ⁵) in the Weyl basis, the two halves of the Dirac spinor transform under distinct copies of SU(2) in the massless limit.

In the massless limit, these two chiralities decouple completely; they transform under independent copies of SU(2). With mass, the two chiralities couple. The coupling strength is the Compton frequency k = mc/ℏ — the rate at which the McGucken-Principle wavefront dx₄/dt = ic advances the phase of a rest-mass-m standing wave (II.2). This coupling is what mixes left and right Weyl spinors into a single Dirac spinor.

**VI.2 The Form of the γ-Matrices**

The γ-matrices are the operators that intertwine the two chiralities. In the Weyl basis fixed in II.4:


γ⁰ = [[0, 𝟙₂], [𝟙₂, 0]], γⁱ = [[0, σⁱ], [-σⁱ, 0]]


γ⁰ exchanges left and right Weyl components; γⁱ exchanges them with a spatial twist determined by the Pauli matrices.

The anticommutation {γᵘ, γᵛ} = 2ηᵘᵛ 𝟙 is the Clifford algebra of the Minkowski metric derived in II.1 from the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic — the same algebra the first-order Dirac operator must satisfy in order to square to the Klein–Gordon operator derived from the wavefront in II.5–II.6.

**VI.3 The Geometric Meaning**

The γ-matrices are the “switches” between matter’s two x₄-orientations. Because matter is single-sidedly x₄-oriented, but both orientations exist in nature (left-handed and right-handed fermions), a complete description requires objects that can flip between the two. These objects are the γ-matrices. Their algebra is the Clifford algebra of the 4D Minkowski geometry derived in II.1 from the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic — the algebra the Dirac operator squares to in the Klein–Gordon derivation of II.5–II.6 — and their 4×4 matrix form reflects the two-chirality-times-two-spin structure of the McGucken-Sphere standing wave.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**IX.1 Assembling the Pieces**

We now have all the geometric elements needed for the Dirac equation:

- Minkowski signature η = diag(−1, +1, +1, +1) from the i in dx₄/dt = ic (II.1)
- Matter as x₄-standing wave with Compton frequency (II.2)
- Clifford algebra {γᵘ, γᵛ} = 2ηᵘᵛ (II.3)
- Matter orientation condition (M) as an algebraic constraint on even-grade multivectors (IV.2)
- Half-angle spinor transformation from the theorem that single-sided action uniquely preserves (M) (Theorem IV.3, Section V)
- Two Weyl chiralities from matter’s two x₄-orientations (VI.1)
- γ-matrices as chirality intertwiners (VI.2)
- Antimatter as right-action with explicit C-operator identification verified at the component level (VII, VIII)
- γ⁴ = iγ⁰ derived from signature consistency (VIII.1)
- CPT as 4D geometric inversion (VIII.9)

The wave equation for a matter field ψ carried by x₄-expansion, first-order in all four coordinates, consistent with the Minkowski geometry, coupling the two chiralities via a mass term proportional to the Compton frequency, is:


(iγ^u∂^u - m)ψ = 0


This is the Dirac equation. Every element has been derived:

- The i in front of γᵘ∂ᵘ traces to the i in dx₄/dt = ic
- The γᵘ matrices are the Clifford intertwiners between Weyl chiralities
- The first-order-in-all-four form is forced by coequal treatment of x₄ and x₁x₂x₃
- The mass m is the x₄-rest-frame oscillation frequency (Compton frequency)
- The spinor structure of ψ reflects the half-angle transformation from Theorem IV.3
- Antiparticle solutions correspond to right-action / x₄-reversed propagation, with the explicit identification of the charge-conjugation operator verified in VIII.7
- CPT is automatic 4D inversion symmetry

**IX.2 Comparison to the Algebraic Derivation**

The standard derivation of the Dirac equation demands first-order-in-all-four and Lorentz covariance, solves the resulting algebraic constraints to find the γ-matrices, and discovers spin-½ as a property of the resulting representation. The representation-theoretic double cover is invoked without geometric justification. Antimatter emerges as a reinterpretation of negative-energy solutions, requiring Dirac’s “sea” construction or the Feynman-Stückelberg “particles going backward in time” picture to be made physically sensible. CPT is then proved as a separate theorem requiring Lorentz invariance and locality as independent assumptions.

The Light, Time, Dimension Theory derivation proceeds in the opposite direction. The geometric facts — x₄-expansion, matter’s x₄-orientation (formalized as the algebraic constraint (M)), the unique orientation-preserving single-sided transformation (Theorem IV.3) — are primary. The algebra of the Dirac equation emerges as the mathematical expression of these geometric facts. Spin-½ is a geometric necessity. Antimatter is the immediate geometric meaning of x₄-reversal, verified at the component level in Section VIII. CPT is an automatic consequence of 4D geometric consistency.

Every distinctive feature of the Dirac equation — Clifford algebra, spin-½, SU(2) double cover, two Weyl chiralities, mass as chirality coupling, antimatter, charge conjugation, CPT — is derived from the single principle dx₄/dt = ic.

**2.1 The rate is a generator; the coordinate is its flow**

The canonical statement that dx₄/dt = ic is primitive and x₄ = ict a "mere integrated shadow" is sharpened by an operator-theoretic fact about order.

**Proposition 2.1 (Generator and flow).** *A first-order operator is the infinitesimal generator of a one-parameter group of motions, recovered by exponentiation: e^{a d/dt} f(t) = f(t+a), a translation. A second-order operator generates no such group; its exponential is a smoothing semigroup (a ≥ 0 only), not a translation. Hence the primitive dx₄/dt = ic, being first-order, is a generator whose exponential is the x₄-flow — the motion — while x₄ = ∫ ic dt = ict is the integrated trace of that flow.*

*Proof.* On the eigenfunction e^{kt}, (d/dt)e^{kt} = k e^{kt}, so e^{a d/dt} e^{kt} = Σ_n (ak)ⁿ/n! · e^{kt} = e^{ak} e^{kt} = e^{k(t+a)} (verified by truncated series); thus e^{a d/dt} is the shift.
